title: Our Big Fat Dream Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the booth) open with banter about dreams and recent naps, then deliver a main dream episode covering REM sleep and its discovery, the eye-movement mouse and lucid dreamer studies, dream frequency and length, Freud vs. Jung dream theories, the activation synthesis hypothesis (Hobson and McCarley), Crick's reverse learning idea, dream recall and how to improve it, dream incubation and famous creative dreams (Kekulé's benzene ring, Frankenstein), recurring dreams and nightmares, PTSD nightmare therapy, Parkinson's-related nightmares, sleep paralysis and night terrors, dream symbolism, and precognitive dreams. The episode closes with listener mail from Cliff in Madison, Wisconsin, about Sammy Davis Jr. calling out to a lost audience member at a Las Vegas concert.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the show and the hosts. Chuck describes a nap he took just before recording and a dream he had.

segments.title: Personal dream sharing
segments.summary: The hosts share their dream habits, recurring dreams, a Gilligan's Island dream, and a Rachel Dratch dream. They reference Dazed and Confused.

segments.title: Sleep stages and REM sleep
segments.summary: Chuck outlines the sleep stages and REM sleep. Josh explains that REM sleep was discovered in the 1950s and that dream paralysis is thought to keep people from acting out dreams. He describes the mouse eye-direction study and the lucid dreamer eye-movement study.

segments.title: How often and how long we dream
segments.summary: Chuck says people likely dream multiple times a night, for minutes up to half an hour, and perhaps a couple of hours total. The hosts discuss how dream length is hard to measure.

segments.title: Freud vs. Jung
segments.summary: The hosts compare Freud's view that dreams conceal repressed desires with Jung's view that dreams reveal meaning through mythic archetypes. They note Freud's lasting influence.

segments.title: Activation synthesis hypothesis
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe the 1970s activation synthesis hypothesis, in which dreams are the brain's narrative attempt to make sense of random neural firing during REM sleep, and name Hobson and McCarley as its authors.

segments.title: Characteristics of dreams and Crick's theory
segments.summary: Josh lists dream characteristics such as illogical content, odd sensations, intense emotion, and accepting strange events. Chuck describes Hobson and McCarley's controversial theory. Josh explains Francis Crick's reverse learning idea. The hosts also mention dress rehearsal and emotional processing theories.

segments.title: Dream recall and forgetting
segments.summary: Chuck notes that dream memories fade quickly, with about half forgotten after five minutes. He suggests dream journals and waking during REM. Josh explains that waking people during REM is used in sleep studies, and a joke about Taco Bell fourth meal.

segments.title: Whether everyone dreams and why recall is hard
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether everyone dreams, with researchers waking people in REM to find dream reports. Freud's repression idea is mentioned. Josh describes the hippocampus and neurotransmitters acetylcholine and norepinephrine as reasons for poor dream recall. Chuck lists lifestyle factors that affect recall.

segments.title: Training dream recall and Josh's waking dream
segments.summary: The hosts discuss dream recall training and staying in a dream while waking up. Josh describes waking up directly out of a dream about getting out of a car. Chuck refers to earlier episodes on lucid dreaming and dream sailing.

segments.title: Dream incubation and creative dreams
segments.summary: Josh explains dream incubation. He describes Kekulé's dream of a snake eating its tail that led to the ring structure of benzene. The hosts discuss Mary Shelley and Frankenstein, and songwriters and musicians who said songs came to them in dreams, including Apex Twin's lucid dream music.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts announce a break before the next part of the episode.

segments.title: Do dreams mean anything? Personal stories
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether dreams have meaning. Chuck describes a childhood dream of his grandfather saying he would be okay, and Josh describes a dream that led to a sailing career.

segments.title: Dream symbols and common interpretations
segments.summary: The hosts go over stock dream symbols: teeth falling out, falling, being chased, fire, and being naked in public. Chuck says interpretations depend on culture and personal context, and Josh says this is more pop culture than science.

segments.title: Recurring dreams and nightmares defined
segments.summary: Josh says recurring dreams are common, and recurring unpleasant dreams are rare. Chuck defines a nightmare in sleep research as a dream that wakes you up. Josh recalls the end of Don't Be Dumb.

segments.title: Dream meaning research and PTSD nightmares
segments.summary: Josh cites Siddhartha Ribeiro's argument that recurring dreams show dreams serve a purpose. Chuck says recurring nightmares are common in veterans and people with PTSD, citing a 1998 study of adult nightmare prevalence and Vietnam veterans.

segments.title: Nightmare therapy and nightmares linked to Parkinson's
segments.summary: Josh describes dream therapy for PTSD and recurring nightmares, which trains people to imagine a different ending. He notes nightmares are linked to self-injury and suicide. The hosts discuss genetics and a link between nightmares and Parkinson's disease with dementia.

segments.title: Related episodes: fever dreams, sleep paralysis, night terrors
segments.summary: The hosts mention past episodes on fever dreams, sleep paralysis, and night terrors. Josh and Chuck describe how sleep paralysis and night terrors happen.

segments.title: Premonitions and precognitive dreams
segments.summary: Chuck describes Kathleen Lorna Middleton, a Canadian dreamer who claimed to foresee a South Wales landslide and the assassination of Robert Kennedy. Josh gives scientific explanations such as ambiguity, pattern seeking, and coincidence, and a quantum physics view that allows precognition. Chuck notes that 17 to 38 percent of people report at least one precognitive dream.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sammy Davis Jr. story
segments.summary: Cliff from Madison, Wisconsin writes about his mother losing her table in a dark Las Vegas concert. Sammy Davis Jr. stopped the show to ask, 'Vic, babe, where are you?' and restarted the concert. The hosts thank Cliff and invite more listener stories about loved ones.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give the email address for listener mail and the iHeartRadio production credit.
